summary:
AstroHealth Mission Control is an autonomous edge-AI platform developed for long-duration deep space missions. We built a PyTorch dual-head neural network that performs continuous risk regression and status classification across nine physiological and environmental telemetry parameters, achieving 99.83% test accuracy.

To address the challenge of deep space communications latencies and periodic solar blackouts, AstroHealth integrates personalized astronaut digital twins, rule-based sensor integrity fault detection, and closed-loop countermeasure simulations (such as CO₂ scrubber and O₂ boosts).

This project is critical because astronauts on Artemis or Mars transit cannot rely on real-time medical oversight from Earth. By providing local, interpretable risk forecasting, real-time sensor validation, and blackout-resilient data buffering, AstroHealth empowers crew autonomy, mitigates hardware anomalies, and aligns with NASA-STD-3001 standards to ensure mission safety when every second counts.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

AstroHealth Mission Control is an autonomous edge-AI decision-support system designed for long-duration deep space exploration. The system processes nine physiological and environmental telemetry parameters: Heart Rate, HRV, SpO₂, Respiration Rate, Core Temperature, Ambient CO₂, Cabin Pressure, Radiation Rate, and Sleep Debt.

It operates via a multi-stage pipeline:

  • Sensor Integrity Layer: Evaluates incoming telemetry against physical limits and cross-channel consistency checks to catch missing, corrupted, or drifted sensor data before model evaluation.
  • Personal Digital Twin: Establishes crew-specific baselines (adjusting for individual physiological norms) and continuously tracks baseline deviations.
  • PyTorch Dual-Head Neural Network: Concurrently runs two inference heads—Head 1 predicts a continuous risk score (0–100 scale), while Head 2 classifies status into Nominal, Warning, or Critical bands.
  • Explainable AI (XAI) & Trajectory Projection: Uses gradient-based attribution to highlight top physiological risk drivers and projects near-term health trends.
  • Closed-Loop Subsystem Simulation: Allows crews to test mitigation actions (e.g., CO₂ scrubber flush, O₂ boost, radiation shielding) and view immediate before-and-after risk score impacts.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Local Edge Autonomy: Operates completely onboard without requiring cloud infrastructure or constant Earth connectivity.
  • False-Alarm Prevention: Cross-checks vitals against cabin environmental sensors to prevent false alerts caused by faulty hardware.
  • Actionable Decision Support: Goes beyond passive alerts by simulating countermeasure efficacy before crew deployment.
  • Forensic Auditability: Features automated incident logging and telemetry session exporting (CSV/JSON) for post-mission debriefs and ground sync.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

During deep-space missions (such as Artemis lunar operations or Mars transit), communication delays can reach up to 20 minutes one-way, alongside total solar particle blackout events. Astronauts cannot rely on real-time ground control flight surgeons during acute emergencies.

AstroHealth bridges this gap by transferring medical risk assessment to spacecraft edge microcontrollers, ensuring crew survival, reducing cognitive overload, and maintaining uninterrupted health monitoring during Earth-link blackouts.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming Language: Python 3.10+
  • Deep Learning Framework: PyTorch (torch.nn for dual-head MLP architecture)
  • User Interface Framework: Streamlit (custom dark-theme styling)
  • Data & Analytics: Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Plotly (interactive multi-subplot telemetry and radar charts)
  • Target Hardware: Spacecraft edge microcontrollers (e.g., Raspberry Pi 4 / NVIDIA Jetson Nano class embedded hardware)

5. How is your project creative?

AstroHealth uniquely combines physiological monitoring with environmental telemetry rather than treating human vitals in isolation. Creative highlights include:

  • Dual-Head Architecture: Jointly optimizing risk regression and categorical classification to catch edge cases where single-output models fail.
  • Interactive Blackout Simulation: Demonstrates local event buffering during simulated Earth link losses, showcasing offline resilience.
  • Interactive Countermeasure Feedback: Provides immediate feedback loops showing risk reduction after applying simulated shipboard interventions.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • NASA Standards Compliance: Aligned environmental alert logic and EVA atmospheric screening with NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2 (Human-System Integration Requirements).
  • Human-In-The-Loop Ethics: Established a clear scientific boundary—AstroHealth is an interpretable decision-support demonstrator, maintaining human oversight rather than replacing crew judgment.
  • Robustness & Generalization: Evaluated model behavior under severe 10–20% baseline noise, sensor dropouts, compound stressors, and external research data (PhysioNet / NASA OSDR).

7. SI Intelligence Usage

  • Super Intelligence (SI) tools (Large Language Models) were utilized during the development of AstroHealth Mission Control as an engineering assistant to accelerate Python code architecture (backend.py, frontend.py), PyTorch dual-head model design, synthetic dataset creation (CSV files), and README documentation. No protected NASA branding, logos, or mission flags were generated or modified. Core problem formulation, domain requirements engineering, and NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2 standards alignment were directed by the team.
